Anatomy of the Hip
 CORE
November 12, 2025
Michael Willey, MD (2020–present)
Highlight
Show highlights
FULL VIEW
OUTLINE VIEW
Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Identify the origin, insertion, and innervation of the pelvic/hip muscles.
Describe the vascular supply to the femoral head.
Identify important ligamentous/capsular structures surrounding the hip.
Describe approaches to the hip, relevant anatomy, internervous planes, structures at risk, and
applications.
Osteology
The pelvis is composed of the ileum, ischium, and pubis, which combine to form the
innominate bone.
Important osseous anatomy of the pelvis/hip
Anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS)

1/24

Considered the lighthouse of the pelvis because the ASIS is easily palpable anteriorly and
used as a point of orientation for surrounding structures.
Origin of the sartorius muscle and the inguinal ligament; The tensor fasciae latae (TFL)
origin lies lateral to the ASIS.
Osteotomy of the ASIS is performed for a modified Smith-Petersen approach
Iliac crest
Superior border of the ilium
Serves as the origin of the TFL, external oblique, and latissimus dorsi
Used for autologous bone graft harvest and bone marrow aspiration
Posterior superior iliac spine
Easily palpable prominence of the posterior pelvis
Used for bone graft harvest
Ischial tuberosity
Posterior prominence palpable with the hip flexed or relaxed in extension
Lower portion (medial): origin of the adductor magnus and the sacrotuberous ligament
Upper portion (lateral): semimembranosus, biceps femoris, and semitendinosus muscles
(hamstring muscles)
Ischial spine
Sacrospinous ligament
Origin of the superior gamellus muscle
Greater sciatic notch
Structures that exit the greater sciatic notch above the piriformis tendon
Superior gluteal artery
Superior gluteal nerve
Structures that exit below the piriformis tendon
Mnemonic POPS IQ
Pudendal nerve
Nerve to the obturator internus
Posterior femoral cutaneous nerve
Sciatic nerve
Inferior gluteal artery and nerve
Nerve to quadratus femoris
Lesser sciatic notch
Located below the ischial spine
Obturator internus tendon passes through the lesser sciatic notch

2/24

Pubic tubercle
Medial insertion of the inguinal ligament
Palpable lateral to the pubic symphysis
Musculature
Abductors of the hip
Muscles in this group are innervated by the gluteal nerves (superior and inferior gluteal
nerves)
Gluteus maximus
Origin: posterior ilium above the gluteal crest to the posterior iliac crest, sacrum, coccyx,
and sacrotuberous ligament
Insertion: distributed between the iliotibial band and the gluteal tuberosity through the
tendinous gluteal sling
Motion: extension and external rotation of the hip
Innervation: inferior gluteal nerve
Arterial supply: inferior and superior gluteal arteries
Gluteus medius
Origin: lateral ilium distal to the iliac crest
Insertion: anterior, lateral, and superior greater trochanter
The gluteus medius is the strongest internal rotator of the hip.
Innervation: superior gluteal nerve
Arterial supply: superior gluteal artery
Gluteus minimus
Origin: lateral ilium distal to the gluteal crest
Insertion: anterior/lateral greater trochanter
Motion: abduction and internal rotation of the hip
Innervation: superior gluteal nerve
Arterial supply: superior gluteal artery
TFL
Origin: anterolateral ilium posterior to the ASIS
Insertion: iliotibial band
Motion: stabilizes the hip in extension
Innervation: superior gluteal nerve
Arterial supply: superior gluteal and lateral circumflex femoral arteries

Flexors of the hip1
Iliacus
Origin: iliac fossa and anterior/lateral sacrum
Insertion: lesser trochanter through the psoas tendon
Motion: hip flexion
Innervation: femoral nerve
Psoas
Origin: transverse processes of L1 through L5 and vertebral body of T12 through L5
Insertion: lesser trochanter through the psoas tendon
Motion: hip flexion
Innervation: lumbar plexus L1 through L3
Sartorius
Origin: ASIS
Insertion: anteromedial tibia through the pes anserinus
Motion: flexes the hip and knee; externally rotates the hip
Innervation: femoral nerve
Arterial supply: femoral artery
Pectineus
Origin: pectineal line of the pubis; from the iliopectineal eminence and pubic tubercle
Insertion: pectineal line of the femur
Motion: adducts and flexes the hip joint
Innervation: femoral and obturator nerve
Iliocapsularis2,3
Origin: anterior hip capsule and anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS)
Insertion: just distal to the lesser trochanter (Resource 1; Figure 1)
Function: stabilizes the anterior hip capsule and the femoral head; proposed to be
hypertrophied in dysplastic and borderline dysplastic hips with instability

4/24

Figure 1 Photograph of a cadaver model dissection shows the anterior aspect of the hip. The
iliocapsularis muscle (IC) originates from the anterior inferior iliac spine (AIIS) and the anterior
hip capsule (C). Its insertion is located just distal to the lesser trochanter (LT). (Reproduced with
permission from Babst D, Steppacher SD, Ganz R, Siebenrock KA, Tannast M: The iliocapsularis
muscle: An important stabilizer in the dysplastic hip. Clin Orthop Relat Res 2011;469(6):1728-
1734.)
Quadriceps
Muscles in this group are innervated by the femoral nerve and function as knee extensors. The
rectus femoris also flexes the hip.
Rectus femoris
Origin: straight or direct head from the AIIS and the reflected or indirect head at the 12-
o’clock position of the superior acetabulum
Insertion: quadriceps tendon at the patella
Motion: knee extension and hip flexion
Avulsion of the AIIS and the rectus femoris occurs in forceful, resisted hip flexion activities
(eg, kicking).
Vastus lateralis

5/24

Origin: intertrochanteric line, anterior and inferior greater trochanter, linea aspera, and
gluteal tuberosity of the proximal femur
Insertion: lateral quadriceps tendon
Vastus intermedius
Origin: anterior and lateral surface of the femur, including the lateral intermuscular septum
of the thigh
Insertion: forms deep portion of the quadriceps tendon
Vastus medialis
Origin: intertrochanteric line, spiral line, linea aspera, and medial intramuscular septum
Insertion: medial quadriceps tendon
Adductors of the hip
Adductor longus
Origin: anterior pubic body lateral to the pubic symphysis
Insertion: middle third of the femur linea aspera
Motion: adducts and flexes the hip
Innervation: anterior division of the obturator nerve
Adductor brevis
Origin: anterior/medial inferior pubic ramus just distal to the adductor longus origin
Insertion: superior linea aspera
Motion: adducts and flexes the hip
Innervation: anterior and posterior division of the obturator nerve
Adductor magnus
Origin: inferior ramus
Insertion: gluteal tuberosity of the femur, linea aspera, adductor tubercle
Motion: hip adductor
Innervation: posterior division of the obturator nerve
Gracilis
Origin: inferior pubic ramus medial to the pubic symphysis and lateral to the origin of the
adductor brevis origin
Insertion: medial surface of the tibia at the pes anserinus
Motion: adducts the hip and flexes the knee
Innervation: anterior division of the obturator nerve
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:18 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000529
6/24

Hamstrings
Muscles in this group function to extend the hip and flex the knee. The hamstrings are
innervated by the tibial division of the sciatic nerve.
Semitendinosus
Origin: ischial tuberosity (medial side)
Insertion: medial surface of the tibia at the pes anserinus
Semimembranosus
Origin: ischial tuberosity (lateral side)
Insertion: medial surface of the tibia at the pes anserinus
Long and short head of the biceps femoris
Origin: ischial tuberosity (medial side)
Insertion: fibular head
External rotators of the hip
Piriformis
Origin: lateral/posterior sacrum
Insertion: passes through the greater sciatic notch and inserts at the posterosuperior greater
trochanter
Motion: external rotation of the hip
Innervation: piriformis nerve
Obturator externus
Origin: anterior obturator foramen/membrane
Insertion: posterior/medial greater trochanter (anterior to the insertion of the quadratus
femoris)
Motion: external rotation of the hip
Innervation: posterior division of the obturator nerve
The deep branch of the medial femoral circumflex artery (MFCA) passes posterior to the
obturator externus tendon.
Obturator internus
Origin: internal or posterior obturator foramen/membrane
Insertion: forms the conjoined tendon with the superior and inferior gamelli and inserts on
the posterior greater trochanter distal to the piriformis tendon
Motion: external rotation of the hip
Innervation: nerve to the obturator internus and the superior gemellus
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:18 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000529
7/24

Superior gamellus
Origin: ischial spine
Insertion: forms the conjoined tendon with the inferior gamelli and the obturator internus
muscle
Motion: external rotation of the hip
Innervation: nerve to the obturator internus and superior gemellus
Inferior gemellus
Origin: posterior/medial ischial tuberosity
Insertion: forms the conjoined tendon with the superior gamelli and the obturator internus
muscle
Motion: external rotation of the hip
Innervation: nerve to the quadratus femoris and inferior gemellus
Quadratus femoris
Origin: lateral obturator foramen above the ischial tuberosity
Insertion: quadrate tubercle of the posterior greater trochanter
Motion: external rotation of the hip
Innervation: nerve to the quadratus femoris and the inferior gemellus
Nerves
Sciatic nerve
Originates from the lumbosacral plexus L4 through S3
Exits the sciatic notch anterior/inferior to the piriformis tendon
The orientation of the sciatic nerve in relation to the short external rotator is important for
posterior approaches to the hip.
Along the posterior column of the pelvis, the sciatic nerve is anterior to the piriformis tendon
and posterior to the conjoined tendon and the quadratus muscle (Figure 2)
During exposure of the posterior column of the pelvis via a posterior approach to the hip and
acetabulum, retractors can be placed anterior to the conjoined tendon into the lesser sciatic
notch because the nerve is protected by the conjoined tendon. If a retractor is placed
anterior to the piriformis tendon, the retractor is directly in contact with the sciatic nerve,
increasing the risk of sciatic nerve palsy.

8/24

Figure 2 Photograph of a fresh cadaver model dissection shows the posterior pelvis. The pelvis is
positioned prone. Right is superior, and left is inferior. The gluteus maximus muscle (1) is
retracted posteriorly. The sciatic nerve (2) is coursing anterior to the piriformis tendon (3). The
sciatic nerve is posterior to the conjoined tendon (4) and the quadratus muscle (5). The greater
trochanter (6), gluteus medius muscle (7), and gluteus minimus tendon (8) are marked. (Courtesy
of Michael Willey, MD, Iowa City, IA.)
Femoral nerve
Originates from the lumbosacral plexus L2 through L4
Passes deep between the psoas and iliacus muscles in the muscular compartment deep to the
inguinal ligament
Anterior division
Motor
Sartorius
Pectineus
Sensory
Medial cutaneous nerve of the thigh

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000529
9/24

Intermediate cutaneous nerve of the thigh
Posterior division
Quadriceps muscles
Saphenous nerve
Obturator nerve
Branch of L2 through L4
Passes through the psoas muscle deep to the common iliac vessels and enters the superior
and lateral obturator foramen
Anterior branch
Adductor longus
Adductor brevis
Gracilis
Posterior branch
Adductor magnus
Adductor brevis
Obturator externus
Dysfunction is common after the modified Stoppa approach.
Obturator nerve is at risk with the superior ramus cut during periacetabular osteotomy via a
modified Smith-Petersen approach.4
Superior gluteal nerve
Lumbosacral plexus from L4 through S1
Innervation for gluteus medius, gluteus minimus, and TFL
Exits the greater sciatic notch above the piriformis muscle
Passes between the gluteus medius and minimus muscles
Do not split the abductor tendon more than approximately 5 cm proximal to the greater
trochanter to prevent injury to the superior gluteal nerve.
Inferior gluteal nerve
Lumbosacral plexus from L5 through S2
Exits the greater sciatic notch below the piriformis muscle
Innervation for the gluteus maximus muscle

Vascular Anatomy
MFCA
Primary blood supply to the femoral head
Injury to this vessel from dislocation, fracture, or iatrogenic injury may result in
osteonecrosis.
Branch of the profunda femoris artery (less commonly from the femoral artery)
Three segments: transverse, ascending, and deep
The transverse MFCA courses posteriorly from the profunda femoris between the
pectineus muscle and the iliopsoas tendon.
The inferior retinacular artery branches from the transverse MFCA, forming the inferior
retinaculum of Weitbrecht and providing a secondary blood supply to the femoral head
(medial synovial fold).
Continues proximally as the ascending MFCA posterior (superficial) to the obturator
externus tendon and anterior (deep) to the quadratus femoris muscle
The trochanteric branch of the MFCA exits laterally between the conjoined tendon and the
quadratus muscle.
The deep MFCA lies anterior to the conjoined tendon and the piriformis tendon, the
location at which it becomes intracapsular, serving as the primary blood supply to the
femoral head.
Gautier et al5 and Lazaro et al6 performed anatomic studies of the MFCA ( Resources 2 and
3).
Lateral femoral circumflex artery
Branch of the profunda artery
Provides blood supply to the femoral head during development
As the femoral neck lengthens, the lateral femoral circumflex artery supplies the anterior
femoral metaphysis as the MFCA lengthens with the femoral neck and continues as the
primary blood supply to the femoral head.
Ligaments
Hip capsule ligaments
Iliofemoral ligament
Lateral/superior branch and medial/inferior branch that originate at the inferior ASIS and
insert at the intertrochanteric line of the femur, forming the Y-shaped Bigelow ligament
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:18 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000529
11/24

Stabilizes the hip during extension and external rotation
Interportal or T-capsulotomy performed for hip arthroscopy disrupts the iliofemoral
ligament, allowing for additional external rotation and distraction (larger capsulotomy
results in additional instability)
Repair restores restraint to external rotation and prevents micro-instability
Ng et al7 reviewed capsular anatomy (Resource 4; Figure 3).
Figure 3 Three-dimensional illustration shows the findings of in vitro cadaver model studies on
the effects of capsular conditions and surgical stages, outlining the contributions of the
interportal capsulotomy and T-capsulotomy and the effects of instability, effusion, and cam
morphology. (Reproduced with permission from Ng KCG, Jeffers JRT, Beaule PE: Hip joint capsular
anatomy, mechanics, and surgical management. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2019;101[23]:2141-2151.)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:18 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000529
12/24

Ischiofemoral ligament
Originates at the ischium and the posteroinferior acetabular rim and inserts at the posterior
intertrochanteric line
Stabilizes the hip posteriorly and restrains internal rotation at neutral and in flexion,
adduction, and internal rotation
Pubofemoral ligament
Originates at the anterior/inferior superior ramus and converges with the iliofemoral and
ischiofemoral ligament
Reinforces the inferior capsule and prevents abduction and external rotation during hip
extension
Zona orbicularis
Circular capsular fibers that run perpendicular to the capsular ligaments
Provides restraint to distraction of the hip joint by serving as a collar at the head-neck
junction
Ligamentum teres
Auxiliary, triangle-shaped ligament between the inferior acetabular notch (medial wall of the
acetabulum to the fovea of the femur)
Important for blood supply only during early development of the hip
Small vessels and nerves, potentially for proprioception, pass into the femoral head.
The ligamentum teres is only important for stability if structural instability is present in the
hip joint (dysplasia and severe impingement levering out the hip joint).
Surgical Approaches
Smith-Petersen Approach
Anterior approach that provides exposure to the anterior hip joint and ilium
Indications
Total hip arthroplasty
Irrigation and débridement of septic arthritis
Open reduction of developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)
Pelvic osteotomies and anterior pelvis fracture fixation (modified Smith-Petersen approach)
Patient positioning
Supine or lateral
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:18 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000529
13/24

Flat radiolucent surgical table or fracture-traction table
Surgical planes
Superficial internervous plane
Sartorius: femoral nerve
TFL: superior gluteal nerve
Deep internervous plane
Rectus femoris: femoral nerve
Gluteus medius: superior gluteal nerve
Technique
Longitudinal incision, starting lateral to the ASIS
Superficial dissection
Identify the TFL muscle belly.
Incise the TFL fascia longitudinally. Avoid dissection directly between the interval of the
sartorius and the TFL to avoid injury to the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve (LFCN).
TFL muscle fibers are bluntly dissected from the medial fascia and retracted laterally.
Ligate the ascending branch of the LFCN if identified between the sartorius and the TFL.
Deep dissection
Identify the rectus tendon origin at the AIIS.
Dissect lateral to the rectus tendon to expose the anterior hip capsule. Tenotomy of the
rectus tendon can be performed for additional intra-articular exposure but should not be
performed routinely because the anterior hip capsule can be accessed laterally without
tenotomy of the rectus tendon.
Extensile techniques
Modified Smith-Petersen approach
Used for pelvic osteotomy (periacetabular osteotomy8) and anterior pelvis/acetabulum
fracture fixation (often combined with a modified Stoppa approach for both column or
anterior column fracture fixation9)
For proximal extension, the incision curves more proximal, lateral, and inferior to the iliac
crest.
External oblique muscle fascia is elevated off the lateral ilium.
The iliacus muscle is elevated from the inner pelvis, exposing the internal fossa of the ilium.
The iliopectineal fascia is then elevated, exposing the true pelvis.
Osteotomy of the ASIS is performed, allowing for medial retraction of the sartorius origin
and the inguinal ligament.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:18 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000529
14/24

This provides exposure to the entire anterior column of the pelvis, anterior hip capsule, and
anterior sacroiliac joint.
Structures at risk
LFCN
Exits the inguinal ligament medial to the ASIS. Point of exit through inguinal ligament is
variable.10
Courses anterior to the sartorius tendon and muscle
Multiple branches of the LFCN are present.
Often a posterior/superior branch extending lateral over the TFL is ligated during the
approach,11 resulting in an area of numbness over the anterolateral thigh.
The LFCN is protected by flexing the hip during the approach and performing an osteotomy
of the ASIS rather than tenotomy of the sartorius/inguinal ligament origin during the
modified Smith-Petersen approach.4
Compression of the LFCN resulting in numbness over the anterior thigh is referred to as
meralgia paresthetica.
The anterior approach protects the primary blood supply to the femoral head (MFCA).5,6
The femoral nerve and the sciatic nerve are at risk during the modified Smith-Petersen
approach for periacetabular osteotomy (reported rate in a large multicenter study was
2.1%).12
Instruments
Sagittal saw and Stiletto osteotomes for modified Smith-Petersen approach
Hibbs retractors
Cobra retractors
Hohmann retractors
Watson-Jones Approach
Anterolateral approach to the hip
Indications
Hip arthroplasty (total or hemiarthroplasty)—Patients indicated for hemiarthroplasty
because of femoral neck fracture may benefit from a lower dislocation rate.
Open reduction and internal fixation of femoral neck fractures
Patient positioning
Lateral position
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:18 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000529
15/24

Flat surgical table with or without lateral positioner
Surgical planes
Intra-nervous plane
TFL: superior gluteal nerve
Gluteus medius: superior gluteal nerve
The muscular interval between the TFL and the gluteus medius is used for this approach.
Both muscles are innervated by the superior gluteal nerve. The superior gluteal nerve
enters the TFL near the origin at the iliac crest and is preserved by not dissecting the
interval proximally to the ilium.
Technique
Longitudinal incision, starting posterior to ASIS and extending over the greater trochanter
Superficial dissection
Split iliotibial band oriented over the greater trochanter, extending anterior proximally. The
iliotibial band should be opened anterior to the insertion of the gluteus maximus muscle
fibers.
Deep dissection
Identify the origin of the vastus lateralis at the vastus ridge of the lateral proximal femur
Dissection carried out anterior to the gluteus medius muscle to expose the anterior hip
capsule
The gluteus medius can be handled via a greater trochanteric osteotomy or a subperiosteal
tenotomy to further expose the anterior hip capsule.
Extensile techniques
Proximal exposure is limited by the superior gluteal nerve that typically passes deep to the
gluteus medius 5 cm proximal to the greater trochanter.
Distally, the vastus lateralis muscle can be elevated posterior to anterior to expose the lateral
femur with or without a tenotomy of the vastus lateralis origin at the vastus ridge.
Structures at risk
Limp because of damage to the gluteus medius muscle or the superior gluteal nerve is the
most common complication with the approach.
The lateral femoral circumflex artery must be ligated anteriorly to prevent excessive bleeding
during anterior exposure.
Femoral nerve or femoral artery injury can occur with misplaced retractors anterior to the
hip joint.
Instruments
Curved and straight cobra retractors
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:18 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000529
16/24

Homan retractors
Saw if planning greater trochanteric osteotomy
Nonabsorbable sutures or screws for repair of abductor mechanism
Surgical Hip Dislocation: Gibson Approach
Extensile approach for circumferential exposure of the femoral head, proximal femur, and
articular surface of the acetabulum
Indications
Management of complex femoroacetabular impingement that cannot be addressed via hip
arthroscopy (posterior cam femoral head-neck junction deformities)
Open reduction and internal fixation of femoral head fractures13
Open reduction with direct visualization of transverse or T-type acetabular fractures14
Modified Dunn procedure for reduction of slipped capital femoral epiphysis11
Femoral head reduction osteotomy for Perthes disease15
Patient positioning
Lateral position
Flat surgical table with lateral positioner to stabilize the pelvis
Surgical planes
Superficial internervous plane
Gluteus maximus: inferior gluteal nerve
Gluteus medius: superior gluteal nerve
Deep internervous plane
Gluteus minimus: superior gluteal nerve
Piriformis: nerve to the piriformis
Technique
Longitudinal incision oriented over the greater trochanter, starting midway between the
greater trochanter and the iliac crest and extending just distal to the vastus ridge
Approach
Split iliotibial band longitudinally over the greater trochanter, extending anterior
proximally. The iliotibial band should be opened anterior to the insertion of the gluteus
maximus muscle fibers. The epifascial vessels (branch of the inferior gluteal artery) mark
the anterior border of the gluteus maximus fibers at the iliotibial band.
The vastus lateralis is elevated superficial to the periosteum from posterior to anterior to
the vastus ridge proximally.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:18 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000529
17/24

Interval between the gluteus minimus and the piriformis tendon is opened. Care should be
taken to avoid injury to the anastomosis of the inferior gluteal artery and the deep branch
of the MFCA that lies on the inferior border of the piriformis tendon.
A digastric (gluteus medius and vastus lateralis muscle) step osteotomy or straight
osteotomy of the proximal femur is performed from the greater trochanter to the vastus
ridge. The step cut should extend superficial proximally and deep distally to provide a bone
block to proximal migration of the osteotomized fragment. An incomplete saw cut should
be performed from posterior to anterior, and the osteotomy should be completed with the
use of an osteotome to provide an anterior step cut that prevents anterior migration
(internal rotation) of the osteotomized fragment. These step cuts restrict the abduction and
internal rotation forces from the gluteus medius on the osteotomized fragment.
The most posterior fibers of the gluteus medius are maintained on the intact femur (seat
belt) to prevent injury to the deep branch of the FMCA.
The gluteus medius and gluteus minimus muscles are dissected anteriorly with the
osteotomized fragment, exposing the anterior hip capsule.
A Z-shaped capsulotomy is performed with care to protect the anterior labrum.
With the hip subluxated via traction and the use of a bone hook around the femoral neck,
the ligamentum teres is transected with the use of a long-curved scissors.
With the hip dislocated anteriorly, the entire femoral head and the acetabulum are
exposed.
Structures at risk
The sciatic nerve is at risk with the approach. After opening the iliotibial band, blunt
dissection should be used to open the space posterior to the hip, deep to the iliotibial band.
This allows space for the proximal femur during anterior dislocation and exposure of the
acetabulum. At this point, the surgeon can identify abhorrent anatomy of the sciatic nerve
and protect it if necessary.
The deep branch of the MFCA is at risk during the dissection, osteotomy, and intra-articular
procedures. Care should be taken to understand the anatomy of the artery and protect it
during the procedure.
Instruments
Charnley self-retaining retractors
Curved and straight Cobra retractors
Hohmann retractors
Two sagittal saw blades and Stiletto osteotomes
Bone hook
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:18 AM
AAOS | Anatomy of the Hip
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000529
18/24

Long curved scissors
Burr and femoral head templates for femoral head-neck offset correction
Ludloff or Weinstein-Ponseti Approach
Medial or anteromedial approach to the hip
Indications
Reduction of DDH
Psoas tenotomy
Tumor biopsy or resection in the medial hip
Patient positioning
Supine position
Radiolucent surgical table
Surgical planes
Superficial intra-nervous plane
Adductor longus: anterior division of the obturator nerve
Gracilis: anterior division of the obturator nerve
Deep internervous plane
Adductor brevis: anterior division of the obturator nerve
Adductor magnus: posterior division of the obturator nerve and branches of the sciatic
nerve
Technique
Longitudinal incision over the adductor longus
Superficial dissection
Dissect between the adductor longus and gracilis muscles
Deep dissection
Dissect between the adductor brevis and the adductor magnus
Expose the psoas tendon and the medial hip capsule
The Weinstein-Ponseti modification of this approach for reduction of DDH technically is an
anteromedial approach that involves the use of a transverse incision oriented over the groin
crease to the adductor longus.
The adductor longus muscle is isolated and sectioned.
The anterior branch of the obturator nerve is identified over the adductor brevis and
protected.

The interval between the pectineus muscle and the femoral neurovascular bundle is bluntly

The lesser trochanter is palpated, and the psoas tendon is transected sharply with care to

address intra-articular blocks to reduction of DDH.
Structures at risk
The MFCA traverses the medial side of the psoas tendon and must be protected during
tenotomy.

The iliotibial band is split longitudinally.
The gluteus maximus muscle is identified as it inserts into the iliotibial band and splits to
the first division of the inferior gluteal nerve.
Deep dissection
For hip arthroplasty indications, the short external rotators are elevated from the posterior
femur (anatomy of the sciatic nerve in relation to the short external rotators should be
reviewed).
T-type capsulotomy is performed to allow for posterior hip dislocation.
Extensile techniques
The exposure is easily extended distally to the femur with posterior to anterior elevation of
the vastus lateralis muscle and potential tenotomy at the vastus ridge.
If the approach is used for acetabular fracture fixation, tenotomy of the piriformis and
conjoined tendons is performed.
The tenotomy should be performed 1 to 2 cm from the insertion to protect the deep branch
of the MFCA.
The sciatic nerve passes anterior to the piriformis tendon and posterior to the conjoined
tendon.
Structures at risk
Sciatic nerve
The sciatic nerve is oriented anterior to the piriformis and posterior to the conjoined
tendons and the quadratus muscle. Care should be taken to perform retraction anterior to
the piriformis tendon to prevent retractor placement directly on the sciatic nerve.
Superior gluteal artery
The superior gluteal artery exits the greater sciatic notch with the sciatic nerve. Retraction
of the superior gluteal artery may result in excessive blood loss via this approach. This is
primarily a risk during surgical fixation of acetabular fractures.
Instruments
Charnley self-retaining retractors
Cobra retractors
Hohmann retractors
Nonabsorbable sutures for repair of the posterior capsule and the short external rotators to
reduce the risk of posterior dislocation
